text: Why are GPUs the default hardware for training large neural networks, even though they were built for graphics?
options: Because they accelerate the linear algebra involved
Because they have fast serial integer arithmetic
Because they use very little power per computation
Because they have large caches for text corpora
answer: Because they accelerate the linear algebra involved
explanation: Every layer of a neural network is a matrix multiply, and GPUs are thousands of cores doing the same operation on thousands of elements at once. Drawing triangles turned out to be the same shape of problem, which is one of the luckiest accidents in the history of computing.

text: Which Google chip is an application specific integrated circuit built specifically for neural network workloads?
options: The Neural Processing Unit
The Tensor Processing Unit
The Tensor Core
The Field Programmable Gate Array
answer: The Tensor Processing Unit
explanation: Google started using TPUs internally in 2015 and opened them to third parties through its cloud in 2018. TensorFlow, JAX and PyTorch all support them, and the distinction from an NPU is mostly that Google calls its own product a TPU.

text: What does CUDA stand for?
options: Central Unified Data Access Unit
Common Universal Deep Architecture
Compute Unified Device Architecture
Compiled Universal Device Accelerator
answer: Compute Unified Device Architecture
explanation: Nvidia created it in 2004 and released it in 2007, and it is a platform and API rather than a chip. It is also the reason Nvidia is hard to displace, since the software ecosystem built on it is decades deep and a competitor has to beat the hardware and the tooling at once.

text: High Bandwidth Memory stacks DRAM dies vertically. Which three companies first developed the standard?
options: Intel, AMD and Nvidia
TSMC, Samsung and Micron
Nvidia, Google and Samsung
Samsung, AMD and SK Hynix
answer: Samsung, AMD and SK Hynix
explanation: It is a 3D stacked SDRAM interface, and the first HBM chip came from SK Hynix in 2013. Training is frequently memory bandwidth bound rather than compute bound, which is why the HBM supply chain became a chokepoint for the whole industry within about two years.

text: Nvidia's Hopper microarchitecture is designed primarily for which workload?
options: Datacenter workloads
Smartphone inference
Consumer graphics cards
Automotive navigation
answer: Datacenter workloads
explanation: Hopper is a datacenter part and sits alongside Lovelace, which is the consumer line. The name comes from Grace Hopper, the naval rear admiral, and the H100 built on it is the chip most of the 2023 to 2025 training runs were done on.

text: Nvidia's Ampere GPU microarchitecture is named after which person?
options: Grace Hopper
Andre-Marie Ampere
Marie Curie
John von Neumann
answer: Andre-Marie Ampere
explanation: The French physicist and mathematician after whom the ampere is named, and Nvidia announced Ampere in May 2020. Nvidia does this consistently, since Blackwell, Hopper and Ampere are all people, and the convention is one of the easier ways to place a card in a timeline.

text: Which company builds the wafer scale engine, a processor built by linking many dies across a single silicon wafer?
options: Graphcore
SambaNova
Cerebras Systems
Groq
answer: Cerebras Systems
explanation: Cerebras in Sunnyvale, California builds a processor the size of a wafer and the CS-3 supercomputers around it, and sells access by API as well. The bet is that model parallelism beats the difficulty of getting a single enormous chip manufactured reliably.

text: An NPU, also called an AI accelerator, is best described as what?
options: A general purpose CPU with a wider instruction set
A type of DRAM stacked in three dimensions
A compiler that targets GPUs instead of CPUs
A specialised hardware accelerator for AI workloads
answer: A specialised hardware accelerator for AI workloads
explanation: It can be standalone, part of a CPU or part of a GPU, and the term is a category rather than a product. The whole category grew out of the observation that neural network inference does a small number of operations very many times, which is a different shape of problem from general purpose computing.

text: Moore's law says the number of transistors on an integrated circuit does what over time?
options: Doubles roughly every two years at near constant cost
Halves roughly every five years at rising cost
Triples every decade at falling cost
Doubles every decade at constant cost
answer: Doubles roughly every two years at near constant cost
explanation: Moore published it as an observation in 1965, not a law, and it described an empirical relationship rather than a physical necessity. It is also the reason people believed AI scaling would be affordable, since compute was on an exponential curve even when the models were not yet good enough to use.

text: Nvidia was founded in 1993 by Jensen Huang and two co-founders. What were the other two names?
options: Jackie Hu and Morris Chang
Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem
Gordon Moore and Robert Noyce
Marc Andreessen and Andy Bechtolsheim
answer: Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem
explanation: The three founded Nvidia after leaving Sun Microsystems, and the company nearly ran out of money in its first few years. Jensen Huang is the one who stayed famous enough to be the answer to a different question, which is the last question on the founders list.

text: Which foundry manufactures most of Nvidia's AI chips and was founded in 1987 by Morris Chang?
options: Samsung
Intel
GlobalFoundries
TSMC
answer: TSMC
explanation: TSMC pioneered the pure-play foundry model and fabs Nvidia's datacenter GPUs, including Blackwell on its 4NP process. Samsung is the tempting miss because it also fabs advanced chips, but Nvidia's AI lineup runs overwhelmingly through TSMC.

text: Which company is the sole supplier of extreme ultraviolet lithography machines for advanced chips?
options: Nikon
ASML
Canon
Applied Materials
answer: ASML
explanation: The Dutch firm ASML holds a near-monopoly on EUV systems printing 5 nm and 3 nm layers at 13.5 nm wavelength. Nikon is the tempting miss because it once led lithography with Canon, but neither ships EUV machines today.

text: Nvidia's Blackwell architecture is named after which person?
options: David Blackwell
Grace Hopper
Andre-Marie Ampere
Ada Lovelace
answer: David Blackwell
explanation: David Blackwell was the statistician behind game theory and probability work that underpins modern ML, honored at GTC 2024 with the B200 datacenter accelerators. Grace Hopper is the tempting miss because Hopper is the preceding Nvidia architecture, also named for a person.

text: Which Nvidia chip became the workhorse of AI training during the 2022 to 2024 boom?
explanation: The Hopper-based H100 powered most frontier training runs of the boom, succeeding the Ampere A100. The A100 is the tempting miss because it was the previous workhorse, but by 2023 waitlists and headlines all pointed at H100 supply.

text: How many GPUs did Nvidia's DGX-1 contain, the system whose first unit was delivered to OpenAI in 2016?
explanation: The DGX-1 packed 8 Pascal P100 GPUs linked by NVLink, and Jensen Huang hand-delivered the first box to OpenAI. Sixteen is the tempting miss because later DGX generations scaled up, but the original 2016 box held eight.

text: What does the LPU in Groq's chip name stand for?
options: Linear Processing Unit
Logic Propagation Unit
Latency Prediction Unit
Language Processing Unit
answer: Language Processing Unit
explanation: Groq rebranded its tensor streaming chip as the Language Processing Unit for LLM inference, and its 2024 speed demos went viral. Linear Processing Unit is the tempting miss because it sounds like standard hardware jargon, but the official expansion is Language, which also fueled confusion with xAI's Grok chatbot.

text: Most advanced AI chips are fabbed in Taiwan. Which of these follows from that concentration?
options: A disruption there would affect only consumer devices
A disruption there could trigger a worldwide chip shortage
A disruption there would make AI models cheaper to train
A disruption there would remove the need for new chip designs
answer: A disruption there could trigger a worldwide chip shortage
explanation: One company on one island makes the dies for the accelerators every AI lab rents, and a fabrication plant takes years to build, so the capacity cannot be replaced quickly if it stops. That dependency is expensive for everyone else to escape, which is the idea behind Taiwan's silicon shield. TSMC is spreading capacity to Arizona partly to soften exactly this risk.
answerAliases: a disruption could cause another worldwide chip shortage
commanding majority in the semiconductor foundry market

text: ASML makes the only machines in the world that can print the smallest features on a chip. Which of these follows?
options: Chipmakers can make the same nodes with older machines
Chipmakers no longer need to buy lithography equipment
Chipmakers can copy the machines once patents expire
Chipmakers at the smallest nodes buy from one supplier
answer: Chipmakers at the smallest nodes buy from one supplier
explanation: EUV is the only way to print the layers at 5 nm and 3 nm, so every advanced chipmaker queues for the same supplier. The dependency is concrete: Intel put $4.1 billion into ASML in 2012 for a 15 percent stake, and Samsung and TSMC took smaller stakes under the same program, so the customers helped pay for the tool they all need. Nikon and Canon once led lithography, but neither ships EUV machines.
answerAliases: the world's only manufacturer of extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography machines
required to manufacture the most advanced semiconductor chips
largest supplier to the semiconductor industry

text: Phone chips from Apple, Qualcomm and Samsung now carry a dedicated neural network accelerator. What is it mainly for?
options: Running small AI models efficiently on low power
Training large language models from scratch on the phone
Replacing the graphics chip used to render phone games
Compressing photos and video to save phone storage
answer: Running small AI models efficiently on low power
explanation: On a phone the accelerator is deliberately small and power-efficient, sized to run little models rather than train them, and a phone running a large model on its main cores would be hot and flat within minutes. Keeping the work on the device also means the data never has to leave the phone. Data centre accelerators make the opposite bet: far bigger, and happy to be noisy.

text: Nvidia paid $6.9 billion for Mellanox, closing the deal in 2020. What did it get that mattered for AI clusters?
options: A chip foundry that could manufacture its own silicon
A competing AI accelerator it could rebrand and retire
InfiniBand networking for linking huge GPU clusters
A controlling stake in the ARM instruction set
answer: InfiniBand networking for linking huge GPU clusters
explanation: Mellanox built InfiniBand adapters and switches, the fabric that stitches thousands of GPUs into a single training job instead of leaving them a room of separate boxes. InfiniBand competes with Ethernet for that job, and having both under one roof is why a cluster is now sold as a system rather than as chips. The company was folded into Nvidia's networking division, and the Mellanox name disappeared from new products.
answerAliases: based on InfiniBand and Ethernet technology

text: Groq and Grok are two different AI things that get mixed up constantly. Which pairing is right?
options: Grok is the chip company, Groq is the chatbot
Groq is the chip company, Grok is the chatbot
Groq is the chatbot, Grok is the chip company
Both are the same company, spelled two ways
answer: Groq is the chip company, Grok is the chatbot
explanation: Groq builds the inference accelerator it calls the LPU, originally a Tensor Streaming Processor, and its speed demos went viral. Grok is the chatbot and model family from SpaceXAI, named after the verb in Heinlein's Stranger in a Strange Land. The one-letter gap between the two names is why they get crossed so often.
answerAliases: builds an AI accelerator application-specific integrated circuit
American artificial intelligence (AI) company that builds

text: An AI accelerator's HBM sits on the same package as the GPU and is joined to it over a link more than a thousand bits wide. What does that width buy?
options: Little, since AI chips are limited by compute rather than bandwidth
A wide path, so weights reach the GPU's arithmetic units faster
Enough capacity to hold a whole model's weights on one card
A cheaper way to build memory than ordinary DDR modules
answer: A wide path, so weights reach the GPU's arithmetic units faster
explanation: A single HBM stack presents a 1024-bit bus to the chip sitting next to it, where a single graphics memory channel is 32 bits, and the dies in the stack are wired together through silicon vias. The point is supply rate rather than storage: a GPU full of arithmetic units sits idle if the weights arrive slowly. Capacity is a separate figure and more layers do raise it, but that is not why the bus is so wide.
answerAliases: The HBM memory bus is very wide in comparison to other DRAM memories such as DDR4 or GDDR5
higher bandwidth than DDR4 or GDDR5
a width of 1024 bits in total

text: HBM, the memory stacked onto AI accelerators, comes from a very small group of suppliers. Which of these four companies is one of them?
options: Kioxia
Nanya Technology
Western Digital
SK Hynix
answer: SK Hynix
explanation: Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron make almost all of the world's HBM, which is why the same three names turn up on every accelerator data sheet. The other names here are storage companies rather than HBM suppliers: Kioxia and Western Digital live in flash, and Nanya makes conventional server DRAM without an HBM line. HBM earns more per wafer than DDR5, so the AI boom has squeezed ordinary DRAM supply as a side effect.
answerAliases: SK Hynix, Samsung Electronics, and Micron Technology

text: The 'double' in the name DDR5 memory refers to what?
options: Data moving on both edges of the clock signal
The number of memory banks inside each chip
The number of bits stored in each memory cell
The rate at which a module refreshes its stored data
answer: Data moving on both edges of the clock signal
explanation: DDR stands for double data rate: the memory moves data on the rising and falling edges of the clock, so a 100 MHz bus is sold as 1600 MT/s. That is why an advertised module speed is twice the physical clock, and the doubling has nothing to do with cells or banks. DDR5 also happens to have two 32-bit subchannels per module, a separate change that confuses anyone reading a spec sheet.
answerAliases: transferring data on both the rising and falling edges of the clock signal
both the rising and falling clock edges

text: A rack full of AI accelerators pumps coolant through cold plates bolted to the chips instead of just blowing room air over them. How does the heat leave the chip?
options: Chilled air pumped up from under the data centre floor blown across the die
Liquid metal filling the plate soaks up the heat like a sponge and holds it
Coolant flowing through the plate absorbs the heat and carries it away
The coolant boiling on contact and its vapour lifting the heat off the die
answer: Coolant flowing through the plate absorbs the heat and carries it away
explanation: A pump pushes coolant through a water block bonded to the chip and out to a heat exchanger, which is the same loop a water cooled car engine runs. Water shifts heat far better than air, and AI racks need it because a full rack of accelerators has gone past what fans can move: immersion designs are rated near 100 kW per 19-inch rack where air cooling stops around 23 kW. Liquid metal fills the gap between chip and plate, and boiling coolant belongs to two phase immersion, neither of which is the cold plate loop.
answerAliases: the water being circulated by a water pump through a water block mounted on the CPU
out to a heat exchanger, typically a radiator
Direct Liquid Cooling (DLC) with cold plates for cooling chips in servers

text: Data centre operators quote a figure called PUE when they talk about how efficiently a building runs. What does that number measure?
options: The share of a data centre's power spent on cooling instead of computing
How efficiently the servers themselves turn electricity into useful work
How much power a data centre draws per terabyte of data it stores
A facility's total power draw divided by the power its computing gear uses
answer: A facility's total power draw divided by the power its computing gear uses
explanation: PUE is total facility energy divided by the energy that actually reaches computing equipment, and a perfect building would score 1.0. Anything that is not a server, an accelerator or a network switch counts as overhead, cooling and lighting included, so a PUE of 1.2 means twenty percent extra energy burned on everything else. It says nothing about how well the chips themselves turn power into useful work, which is the gap researchers were complaining about when they proposed compute-centric metrics instead.
answerAliases: PUE is the ratio of the total amount of energy used by a computer data center facility to the energy delivered to computing equipment

text: A chip designer draws up the blueprints and leaves the making to someone else. What is a chip foundry there to do?
options: A company that designs chips and licenses them to be built
A factory that makes chips from other companies' designs
A plant that buys finished chips and resells them under its own label
A company that assembles finished chips into laptops and servers
answer: A factory that makes chips from other companies' designs
explanation: A foundry is the factory: it owns the clean room and the process, and turns somebody else's design into silicon, which is why it is also called a fab. Pure-play means it does not draw up chip designs of its own, so TSMC can build chips for Nvidia and AMD without competing with them. The older arrangement was the integrated device manufacturer, which designed and fabbed under one roof, and the rise of fabless companies like Nvidia is what split those two jobs apart.
answerAliases: also called a fab or a foundry, is a factory where integrated circuits (ICs) are manufactured

text: Extreme ultraviolet lithography is the process behind the smallest features on modern chips. What does the machine actually do to a wafer?
options: Shoots ions into the wafer to change how it conducts
Etches material between layers to cut the vertical features
Cuts each finished chip out of the wafer surface
Projects a circuit pattern onto a light sensitive coating
answer: Projects a circuit pattern onto a light sensitive coating
explanation: EUV is a light source: it projects a circuit pattern onto a light sensitive coating called photoresist, and later steps copy that pattern down into the silicon. The light sits at 13.5 nm, a band ordinary lenses cannot carry at all, so the optics bounce it off mirrors instead of refracting it through glass. Ion implantation and etching are genuine steps in the same factory and dicing happens at the very end, but none of them is lithography.
answerAliases: create intricate patterns on semiconductor substrates
to produce a pattern by using a reflective photomask to expose a substrate covered by photoresist

text: The smallest process nodes, the ones AI accelerators are built on, come out of foundries run by the same three companies. Which three?
options: TSMC, Samsung and Intel
TSMC, SK Hynix and Micron
GlobalFoundries, UMC and Tower
Intel, UMC and Tower Semiconductor
answer: TSMC, Samsung and Intel
explanation: TSMC, Samsung and Intel are the three that operate foundries at the smallest nodes, and every recent generation from 7 nm down has been built by those same names. GlobalFoundries, UMC and Tower are real foundries that deliberately stopped short of the newest nodes, because a plant for them costs billions and their customers do not need them. Intel is also the company that quietly dropped the nanometer suffix from its node names, calling its newest process 18A instead.

text: A chipmaker advertises a chip built on a 3 nm process. What does that label actually tell you?
options: A physical size, with the smallest feature at 3 nm
The area the finished chip covers on the die
The generation of process it belongs to, not a size
The switching speed of one transistor, in nanoseconds
answer: The generation of process it belongs to, not a size
explanation: Nothing on the chip measures 3 nm any more: the name has been a generation label rather than a physical size for years, and the figure matches no gate length or metal pitch at all. What it does reliably mean is more transistors packed into the same area, built with more machines and more process steps. The sharpest reminder is that TSMC and Samsung shipped the same 3 nm label on very different transistors, FinFETs for one and gate-all-around for the other.
answerAliases: no direct relation to any actual physical feature
used primarily as a marketing term
new, improved generation of silicon semiconductor chips

text: TSMC sells CoWoS as advanced packaging for AI accelerators. What does it do?
options: Prints the transistor layers at a tighter node than a fab
Tests every die and discards the ones that fail
Cuts a finished wafer into separate chips for shipping
Merges several dies into one package as a single device
answer: Merges several dies into one package as a single device
explanation: Advanced packaging puts two or more dies into one package and wires them together so that the pair behaves like a single chip, and CoWoS does it over an interposer that carries the connections. It exists because shrinking one monolithic die keeps getting harder, so the industry bought performance back by connecting dies instead of drawing more of them. Dicing the wafer and sorting the good dies are real steps too, but they bracket this one rather than being it.

source.title: Advanced packaging (semiconductors)

answerAliases: TSMC's CoWoS (chip-on-wafer-on-substrate) technology, which uses an interposer
to be merged and packaged as a single electronic device
combining logic (processors) and memory in a single package
